This glossary is being developed and will gradually include key Workbook terms as they appear.

Agent of change

An individual, group, or organisation capable of exercising agency to influence the direction of change. Agency refers to the ability of an actor to become relevant within a particular context and to shape actions.
Source: 

Simoens et al., 2022, following 

Leipold & Winkel, 2017's definition (p. 524). First introduced in: See 

Paragraph

Service design

A service is the way in which an organisation, through people, processes, technologies, and environments, enables someone to achieve a desired outcome, thereby creating value through that interaction.
Source: To add. First introduced in: See 

4.1 Beyond human-centred design

Sustainability or survivability

Sustainability focuses on long-term well-being, whereas survivability focuses on the capacity to endure and meet immediate needs under challenging conditions. Both are shaped by interconnected social, economic, and environmental factors.
Source: 

Halawa, 2024. First introduced in: See 

Paragraph

Sustainable transitions

Processes of changing unsustainable systems and practices
towards more sustainable ways of living.
See also 

Societal transformation.

Societal transformation

Fundamental changes in social structures, institutions,
behaviours, and relationships.
Related concept: 

Sustainable transitions.

records.content:
This Cross-boundary Workbook of the City as A Laboratory project is the result of a joint effort by TU Berlin, Politecnico di Milano and TU Delft within the ENHANCE Alliance of European Universities of Technology. It is an open-access resource that supports reflective practice by encouraging learners to critically examine their experiences, intended actions, and assumptions, strengthening transdisciplinary learning and the co-creation of knowledge from, for, and with society. As such, the Workbook encourages citizens including students, educators, practitioners, policymakers and community members to collectively address interconnected social, economic, and environmental challenges.

The Workbook consists of six learning modules, each with its own reference list and tasks with customisable worksheets for hands-on practice. Learners can compile their work into a Learning Journey Portfolio and use a glossary of terms shared across all modules as a reference. Each module combines theoretical insights with audiovisual explainers, case studies, and tasks developed by contributing authors working across disciplinary and societal boundaries. Cases present real-life examples of collaboration, while tasks offer transferable learning activities that learners can apply in their own contexts. Together, the modules create opportunities to connect, explore ideas, reflect, and exchange experiences through learning and transformation events that learners can join or organise themselves.

By integrating diverse perspectives and forms of knowledge, this Workbook strengthens learners’ ability to navigate complexity and supports the co-creation of sustainable practices across disciplines, sectors, and cultural contexts.

Explain the motivation, structure, expected use, contributions to and benefits from this Workbook.

Define key concepts such as change, transition, transformation and sustainability mean to you.

Develop the willingness to apply the Workbook content to your personal development by starting to compile a Learning Journey Portfolio.

An invitation to share knowledge, collaborate, and learn from each other to achieve individual and societal goals. This motivation lies at the heart of the Workbook.



Figure 1:Gap between the imaginary of the “City as a Laboratory” and current situation. Visual by Ariele Empirio.

As a citizen of this world, whether affiliated with an academic, government, business, cultural or civil society organisation, you may see yourself in 

Figure 1, perhaps curious about your role as an 

agent of change. In this role, you may be concerned with 

sustainability or survivability challenges.

At one extreme, people with basic comfort and liveability face sustainability challenges, understood as interconnected social, economic, and environmental issues that affect long-term well-being. On the other extreme, those experiencing multiple scarcities (e.g., housing, food, energy, and water) struggle with survival due to limited access to resources. While in some societies the differences between these extremes are greater, both groups can be found worldwide, contributing to environmental degradation for different reasons: the former through overconsumption and waste, and the latter through a lack of technological and economic means to use resources sustainably 

Halawa, 2024. As a result, each group experiences the consequences of challenges such as climate change, biodiversity loss, migration, urbanisation, and threats to sustainability and democracy in different ways, depending on their circumstances. In this context, one can understand “democracy” (†see glossary) as the meaningful participation of citizens in decision-making, which also implies that responsible citizens actively engage in shaping acceptable standards and inclusive futures for all, regardless of group affiliation ( Ribeiro et al, 2025↗ ). Although values like sustainability and democracy are often framed as universal or long-term goals, this can lead to one group imposing them on others, overlooking cultural differences and failing to acknowledge their own limitations in addressing complex challenges. Accordingly, interventions should not be transferred uncritically between contexts; they require adaptable and flexible design that accounts for evolving values and needs over time ( Davis & Nathan et al 2015↗ ).

Similarly, in the places where you live, study or work, you may observe or personally experience somehow unequal access to basic living standards within and across neighbourhoods and social groups. You may have noticed that tensions between shared and private resources often amplify inequalities and lead to conflicts between identities and competing visions of the future. This awareness may motivate you to imagine more equitable, ethical, and responsible ways of thinking and acting, both individually and collectively. At the same time, you may wonder whether it is possible or worthwhile to address today’s complex challenges without sufficient resources or a clear role in decision-making within your community or organisation. You may also simply not know where to begin or how to make a meaningful difference.

These reflections may lead to a broader question about your own role in addressing such challenges. Hence, do you see yourself as a change- or transition-maker? Keep in mind that “change”  (†see glossary) is not only the result of moving from one situation to another which may not always be desired. Change is also an ongoing process that unfolds across different spatial and temporal scales, with or without your involvement ( Mierlo & Beer, 2020↗ ).

When referring to change toward a desired state of sustainability, and to avoid labeling societies as developed or underdeveloped, the term “sustainable development” (†see glossary) has gradually been replaced by “sustainable transitions” (†see glossary) or “transformations”, although these terms do not carry the same meaning. To begin with, a “societal transition” refers to large-scale changes in how society thinks and acts. These transitions can result from abrupt events that disrupt the status quo, prompting groups to respond with solidarity and reinforce existing identities. They may take time to unfold as practices change and identities are reshaped ( Janssen et al., 2022↗ ). To become “sustainable”, transitions should be inclusive or representative to all societal groups . In the process, one must admit that “sustainable transformations” (†see glossary) are transformative visions of the future shaped by whose perspectives and comfort levels define the challenge, as well as by the identities, values and positions of those involved ( Halawa, 2024↗ ). As illustrated in the podcast suggested for the practical exercise of this module ( see below Task 1.2. what does sustainability mean to you? ), researchers from various fields discuss how actions considered sustainable in one place may worsen conditions for other groups of the (world’s) population.

Given this complexity and plurality of perspectives, engaging in societal transitions and transformations whether sustainable or not requires continuous learning and reflection. Therefore, this Workbook is intended to support you in designing the change you seek in your own life. In doing so, you can rethink your role and responsibilities as a transition-maker through a learning journey that encourages you to explore complex challenges and experiment with new ways of thinking and acting, both individually and collectively.  To support your learning, we invite you to revisit your personal development plan and compile your work and experiences from the Workbook modules you follow in your own context into a “Learning Journey Portfolio” (†see glossary).

This Workbook further encourages you to go through this journey with a cooperative, and hopeful yet critical attitude:

Lasting change takes time. It often begins with you, but it is not only about you. Take time to understand the challenges, imagine ways to address them, and view tensions and conflicts as opportunities to learn and adapt. Exchange perspectives with others along the way.

Start small but act with purpose. Choose wisely when to act about these challenges and when not to, based on your role and resources. Acting includes both small steps, like building connections, but also refraining from action or even doing nothing for now. Transformation efforts also require caring for yourself and your loved ones, so you are ready to act when it matters most.

Every result holds a lesson. Reflect on your learning journey, including both process and results for yourself, others, society, and the environment. Consider feedback (e.g. reactions, ideas, beliefs) to support your well-being and personal growth.

records.content: Cities are key centres of human activity, creativity, and knowledge and major contributors to interconnected social, economic, and environmental challenges. At the same time, they bring diverse people together, making them places to collaborate and explore alternative ways of thinking and acting. Do you perceive your city, village or community or the spot where you work, learn and live as a space to change everyday practices, live as yourself with others, and develop sustainable ways of living? This module elaborates on the City as a Laboratory and guides you through seven tasks to help revisiting and sharing how did you connect and define with a real-life example of a challenge that as a basis for developing and refining your learning journey as illustrated through an individual portfolio, parts of which you will share with others.

To write subtitle.



Figure 1:Gap between the imaginary of the “City as a Laboratory” and current situation. Visual by Ariele Empirio.

By following the metaphor of the “City as a Laboratory”, this Workbook invites you to see cities not simply as places that grow “on their own.” Instead, this module encourages you to imagine cities as shared places and projects where everyone, not just a few, can take part, make their own choices, and influence what happens by sharing their ideas, hopes, and skills 

Saunders, 2010

Philipp & Jende, 2025.

In the imagined view shown in 

Figure 1, the term “city” is not about size or location, but about places where people try to live their own lives together with others in fair and supportive conditions while learning from one another 

Philipp & Jende, 2025. In this imaginary, being part of a place means more than simply living there. It means being part of a community.

Research on pre-industrial understandings of dwelling suggests that the French term habiter and the English notion of dwelling imply more than simply residing in a place. They point to an active social life within a community and an ongoing relationship with one’s environment. People shape places, and places shape people 

Henri & Donald, 1991.

However, consumer lifestyles and entertainment industries have often transformed cities into spaces centred on commercialised public areas and high levels of consumption 

Wilson & Erk, 2023. While this development has supported economic growth, it also contributes to excessive resource use, emissions, and waste, while affecting well-being through stress, overwork, inactivity, individualism, and social isolation 

Kronenberg et al., 2024.

Explore and recognise the underlying values leading to dignified learning.

By Fatima-Zahra Abou Eddahab-Burke

Under preparation

Add caption

Who gets to define a city’s challenges, whose knowledge counts, and who can influence what happens next? This module explores why human dignity matters when people learn and act together across neighborhoods, organizations, and communities. In cities where access to resources and decision-making is uneven, the way a learning pathway is designed can reinforce those inequalities or create more meaningful opportunities to participate. Designing for dignity starts from the equal worth of everyone involved and asks what conditions allow people to contribute on their own terms and shape decisions that affect them. Through the values-at-risk methodology and the dignity-based design cycle, you will examine a challenge in your city, trace how different groups experience it, and identify the values and underlying values of dignity shaping current responses. You will bring diverse perspectives into dialogue, explore where values align or come into tension, and use design for values methods to turn those insights into choices about how people learn and act together. In your Learning Journey Portfolio, you will propose a pathway for dignified learning and action. You will explain whose perspectives informed it, how your design could address barriers to participation and strengthen relationships, and what could help the value you create together endure beyond the immediate collaboration.

Explain why values matter in setting up cross-boundary collaboration.

Explain why dignity matters to participate, contribute, and influence decisions.

Use design-for-values approaches to analyse where perspectives align or come into tension.

Design a pathway for dignified learning that strengtens mutual relationships beyond the initial collaboration.

records.content:
To write subtitle.

In the previous chapter “Connect with and define the challenge”, you considered what draws you to a shared challenge, where its boundaries lie, who are its main stakeholder, and what role you could play. The way you defined the challenge already expresses values. If you framed urban heat as a public health issue, you might ask who is most exposed and how to protect them. If you framed it as a question of access to public space, you might ask who can use parks, streets, and squares on the hottest days. Each framing directs attention to particular experiences, brings different people into the conversation, and makes certain responses easier to imagine. Setting up a collaboration gives you a chance to revisit that framing with others.

Video transcript

What is value-based design?

In simple words, it is a way of designing or a design approach that not only starts from, but is based on those guiding principles of our actions as individuals, citizens, or as stakeholders in the organizations that we are representing. In such an approach, we don’t start with the objective, for example, reducing CO2 emissions. We look into why we are actually doing that, and that is the value of sustainability. Here, individually, we reflect on and define our values, what matters the most to us, and collectively, we try to agree on what is that thing that speaks to all of us. It could be one or more values to consider. Agreeing on what people value the most not only broadens the design opportunities, but it also leads to designing systems that are ethical and very much needed by society.

Creating places where people and other living beings can thrive together.

By Francesco Vergani & Valentina Facoetti

Under preparation

Add caption

Cities and everyday environments are often imagined and designed as spaces made by and for humans. Yet they are continuously inhabited, shaped and transformed by plants, animals, fungi, bacteria and other non-human agents. This module introduces More-than-Human and Multispecies Design as approaches for moving beyond Human-Centred approach and reconsidering Design as a relational practice within interconnected ecological worlds. Learners will explore how anthropocentric assumptions shape urban environments and how non-human agency can be acknowledged in city design. Attention is given to living and non-living agents, whose behaviours, needs and capacities are frequently overlooked despite their central role in urban ecosystems. Through data collection, relationship mapping, reversed perspective approach and future envisioning, learners will identify non-human agents, investigate the relations and stressors that shape its everyday conditions and reflect on existing power dynamics. They will therefore transform the insights gathered into a speculative future scenario “beyond the human”, aimed at fostering a mutually beneficial coexistence between the human and non-human worlds. The module encourages participants to document a contextualised multispecies relationship, to critically question anthropocentric assumptions and to propose an possible intervention that is attentive to coexistence, care, temporality and the autonomy of different forms of life.

Recognise the limits of designing only for humans and why it matters to consider other living beings in the design of shared spaces.

Learn to see a place from the perspective of the plants and animals that live there.

Imagine Imagine a future that supports coexistence between humans and nature.

To write subtitle.

Design has always cared about the wellbeing of society (Cooper, 2011). In the 20th century, designers mostly focused their work on the design of functional objects and on testing new materials and production methods. From the 1970s onwards, the focus gradually shifted from industrial profit towards people's interests and needs. It was during this period that human-centred design emerged, an approach that begins by listening to people's needs and experiences. By the late 1990s, design was no longer only about objects. It expanded to services, planning, community development, social innovation, and even experiments in democratic participation (Manzini, 2015). During this period, {term}`service design` became established as the practice of designing services around people's experiences. Services came to be seen as drivers of wider social change (Sangiorgi, 2011), supporting more collaborative, sustainable, and creative societies. This requires inclusive participation, where people take part in discussions and influence collective decisions.

As design engaged with increasingly complex social challenges, human-centred design evolved into community-centred design (Meroni, 2007). Rather than designing for individual users, community-centred design works with groups and communities to create innovative solutions. The focus shifts from individual needs to the collective interests, values, and aspirations shared by a community (

IDEO.org, 2015).

More recently, design has moved beyond a purely human-centred perspective towards approaches that acknowledge the interconnectedness of humans, other species, and ecosystems. Sustainability challenges and nature-based practices have contributed to this shift, paving the way for multispecies design (Roudavski, 2020; Westerlaken, 2020). This approach recognises that plants, animals, and other living beings shape and influence their environments and should therefore be considered in design processes. By fostering collaboration across species, multispecies design aims to create more sustainable and resilient environments and address challenges that human-centred approaches alone cannot adequately address (Forlano, 2017; Giaccardi et al., 2025; Tironi & Garretón, 2024).

Video transcript

What is the de-centering perspective?

So de-centering in general terms means shifting away from having a single perspective at the core of our system, that it’s quite usually the one of the humans. It means acknowledging the fact that perspectives are always partial, situated and not universal. De-centering is a way for us to understand that while in the process of designing we need to care not just for the people, but also the need, the requirements of other entities that are sometimes biological entities like plants, animals and bacteria, but other time non-human entities such as artificial intelligence and machine learning. De-centering doesn’t mean putting away the perspective of the human, but creating spaces for other perspectives. As for transdisciplinary learning, de-centering perspectives might be able to open up to a form of knowledge that it’s ecological, it’s experiential, might be indigenous and not just fixed into an anthropocentric and human body.

hierarchy.lvl2: What does a multispecies approach mean for the design of cities?
What does a multispecies approach mean for the design of cities?

records.content:
When we think about communities, we often think about cities. We tend to see them as spaces made by and for people. However, cities are also shaped by other species such as plants, animals, fungi, and bacteria, as well as by many physical and digital artefacts. Together, these human and non-human actors continuously influence and shape everyday urban life. Still, in much of the Western world, cities have long been imagined as human-made and human-oriented. Plants, animals and other non-human beings were deliberately kept out of social and political life (Escobar, 2019). Ecosystems are so far valued primarily for the services they provide to people, with little consideration for the capacity of other species and ecological systems to regenerate and strengthen the relationships that enable humans and non-human forms of life to flourish together.

The result is that urban ecosystems have been profoundly transformed by human activity, a process called anthropization. Cities are now often inhospitable for both people and other living beings. The UN Sustainable Development Goals 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities) and 15 (Life on Land) draw attention to this problem, which cities are primarily stems from human-centered design, which has shaped urban contexts that are often challenging to navigate particularly in terms of health and well-being.

A multispecies approach invites us to imagine cities differently. Instead of asking “what does this space offer to people?”, we can also ask, "who already lives here, and what do they need?". Streets, parks and buildings become shared habitats rather than human-only places. In recent years, designers, planners and policymakers have started to explore this path. Ideas such as the "Multispecies city" (Houston, 2019) and the "More-than-human city" (Franklin, 2017; Heitlinger et al., 2024) offer new ways of thinking about coexistence, giving importance to the wellbeing and agency of human and non-human beings. Within this context, plants play a crucial role in sustaining urban ecosystems as they provide environmental, social and economic benefits for people. Yet they are still often seen as "ontologically inferior" to humans (Gibson & Baylee, 2018), as if they mattered less because of what they are. Design has long reduced them to resources serving human needs (Sandler, 2018; Turner-Skoff & Cavender, 2019; Višak, 2018). "Critical Plant Studies", a field bringing together environmental humanities, plant sciences, art, philosophy and ethics, questions the idea of plants as passive and voiceless (Plumwood, 2002). It sees them as active agents that shape and respond to their surroundings (Marder, 2013).

Recognising plants, and other non-human lifeforms, capable of being primary contributors in design is a challenge to reshape the role of Design today, that is overly centred on humans. This shift requires a new approach to design, fosters collaboration between multiple species as part of the solution to sustainability challenges, keeping in mind all the consequences that the act of design has for the surroundings and its actors.

Three neighborhood initiatives spanning the major urban areas of The Hague and Rotterdam and the smaller area of Rijswijk.

By Hanneke Bezemer, Axel Birnage, Amila In, Fatima-Zahra Abou Eddahab-Burke & Juliette Cortes-Arevalo

Under preparation

Is investing in biodiversity enough without investing in collaboration?

Municipalities can strengthen biodiversity by prioritising places where ecological and community values are aligned. However, lasting impact depends as much on supporting collaboration as on ecological interventions.

Across the neighborhood initiatives outlined in this case, participants valued diverse expertise but called for stronger evaluation, monitoring, and connections between initiatives to capture learning, broaden participation, and better support biodiversity improvements.

Case: From biodiversity ambitions to local action in Zuid-Holland

records.content:
Biodiversity in Dutch cities, particularly in the densely populated province of South Holland, is declining as urban development and infrastructure continue to fragment the green spaces needed for species to thrive. Yet healthy urban ecosystems can provide cultural benefits such as recreation and community cohesion while also supporting climate adaptation, depending on how they are designed and managed.

To restore and strengthen urban biodiversity, municipalities increasingly invest in neighborhood-based initiatives that engage residents, community organisations, and private actors in environmental stewardship. Such initiatives not only enhance local ecosystems but can also strengthen connections between people and nature. This case explores three initiatives (Figure Case 1-1) located in the major cities of The Hague and Rotterdam and the smaller city of Rijswijk. Their experiences offer inspiration and practical insights for anyone interested in supporting biodiversity through local collective action.

To better understand how to support neighborhood initiatives, the municipalities where these initiatives take place partnered with The Green Village, a field lab under the TU Delft’s Innovation & Impact Centre that connects practitioners and researchers working on climate adaptation innovations. Three bachelor’s theses from TU Delft’s Faculty of Technology, Policy and Management contributed to this effort by examining the strengths and tensions of municipal-community collaborations.

Drawing on policy documents, each thesis compared municipal ambitions with the experiences reported by four initiative participants interviewed between December 2025 and January 2026 to outline key lessons for similar initiatives.

records.content:
Local governments in the Netherlands play a key role in achieving national biodiversity ambitions. Under the National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan 2025–2030, municipalities are expected to contribute to targets such as expanding urban green space, supporting biodiversity friendly design, enabling public participation, and restoring ecosystems. In South Holland, these ambitions are reflected in provincial and municipal policies, including strategies developed by The Hague, Rotterdam, and Rijswijk to strengthen biodiversity at the building, street, and neighborhood scales. For example, Rotterdam aims for all natural areas and ecological zones to meet the Basic Nature Quality standard by 2040, providing habitat conditions that can sustain representative native species. However, municipalities recognise that achieving biodiversity goals cannot rely solely on public land. As much urban space is privately owned, residents, community groups, and local organisations play a crucial role in creating and maintaining green spaces. Community-led initiatives therefore complement municipal efforts by contributing local knowledge, stewardship, and neighbourhood engagement.

At the same time, policy documents acknowledge that residents differ in their interests, capacities, and priorities, which can influence participation. Strengthening native biodiversity consequently requires collaboration among municipalities, professionals, community organisations, and residents, combining technical expertise and local knowledge to develop approaches tailored to the needs and opportunities of each neighbourhood.

records.content:
Municipalities in South Holland such the ones of this case description have introduced measures to support neighbourhood biodiversity initiatives. Residents can access funding for greening projects on private property, challenge municipal plans that may harm biodiversity, and benefit from planning guidelines requiring biodiversity-friendly features in new developments. In principle, these policies create opportunities to enhance urban nature without requiring additional land or major public investments. In practice, however, municipalities struggle to balance biodiversity ambitions with competing priorities. As recognised in Rotterdam’s Biodiversity Framework (2023), housing development, infrastructure upgrades, and the energy transition often take precedence over ecological considerations.

Interviewed municipal actors in Rotterdam and The Hague noted that biodiversity budgets are limited, making both largescale and long-term projects difficult to implement. Physical constraints further reduce opportunities for greening, as streets must accommodate parking and extensive underground networks for water, electricity, gas, and telecommunications.
Decision-making procedures add another layer of complexity. Responsibilities for planning, implementation, and maintenance are distributed across multiple actors, while municipalities increasingly position themselves as facilitators rather than leaders of neighbourhood initiatives. As a landscape architect involved in a collaboration in The Hague observed, nobody is entirely responsible for the success of that project.

“This shared responsibility can encourage participation but may also create uncertainty about accountability and long-term support.”

records.content:
A mostly paved neighborhood in Den Hague

The Scheveningen-Dorp collaboration between the municipality and a residents’ initiative began in 2019. Strong sea winds, combined with the dry air and soil conditions resulting from the neighbourhood’s proximity to the coast led to the commissioning of a landscape architecture firm to develop a “greenery toolbox” aimed at enhancing biodiversity. The toolbox uses street typology and proximity to the sea to identify opportunities for greening. As illustrated in Figure Case 1-2, and provides recommendations on minimum planting areas, plant sizes, and required distances from surrounding infrastructure for each street configuration.

A continuous green corridor on former railway land in Rotterdam-West

Since 2013, residents have initiated and maintained the Spoortuin, a large vegetable garden and woodland corridor within walking distance of Rotterdam Centraal Station. The group managing the area received a grant through a national Dutch campaign supporting neighbourhood initiatives. The municipality now regards the Spoortuin as an example of how residents can self-organise, secure funding, and mobilise volunteers for green-space management. Over time, the group established strategic partnerships to expand community-managed green spaces within Essenburgpark and collaborated with other initiatives to strengthen municipal support. Both projects are located alongside the NS railway and form part of the Groene Connectie, an 8-km green route linking initiatives across Rotterdam (Figure Case 1-3). Together, they connect municipally protected urban nature, water-storage areas, and walking routes with community-managed green spaces.

A small neighborhood park in Rijswijk

The Parkrijk collaboration emerged to develop a 200-squaremetre forest intended to provide habitat for biodiversity while also offering space for the neighborhood and school children (Figure Case 1- 4). The park was completed between 2021 and 2023 with municipality and a non-governmental nature organisation in charge of the planning and implementation. A local school joined during the implementation phase to coordinate educational activities and ongoing maintenance. Although the partners had no prior experience working together, they were enthusiastic and committed throughout the project, except during a transition period when the school's initial representative left the organisation.

records.content:
In the Scheveningen collaboration in The Hague
Despite these efforts, the municipality continued to classify the area as a “paved neighbourhood” with little green space in 2023, while Nature & Milieu (2025) ranked parts of it among the most heat-stressed neighbourhoods in the Netherlands. Implementation has been hindered by limited space for greening, the lengthy process of complying with regulations across multiple responsible organisations, restricted funding, and annual budgeting cycles. Although the toolbox and municipal campaigns promoting garden depaving initially generated momentum, residents’ interest in greening initiatives gradually declined as

In the Rotterdam collaboration,members of the residents’ initiative contributed architectural, legal, political, and ecological expertise to advance the project. Despite this, it took time to align organisational interests and identify synergies, suggesting that progress depends not only on expertise but also on the quality of relationships between actors. Administrative categories further constrained ecological ambitions. As one resident noted, whether a green space is classified as a “forest plot” or a “park” significantly affects how it is managed. Different classifications entail different regulations and management objectives, which can limit opportunities to prioritise biodiversity and make ecological goals secondary to administrative requirements. A fundamental challenge in shifting biodiversity from a subjective aspiration to a measurable policy objective is that indicators for assessing the ecological value of a place remain underdeveloped at the neighbourhood level.

In the Rijswijk collaboration,  the active involvement of the municipality helped make the budget application process smoother for the other partners. Changes in school representatives over time required the collaboration to rebuild relationships and maintain continuity. However, the main challenge was helping less engaged residents recognise the value of biodiversity within the proposed park. People relate to nature in different ways and do not necessarily prioritise biodiversity. A similar challenge was identified in the Rotterdam collaboration. As one resident observed, “People don’t feel that they are allowed to use [green spaces in the neighborhood] […], they don’t feel entitled. They don’t have the sense that it belongs to them”.  The question of how to engage less involved residents in biodiversity and greening initiatives therefore remains an important one for the municipality.

records.content:
Municipalities can strengthen biodiversity by giving it higher priority in policy, funding, and urban development. Multi-year budgets and stronger municipal leadership in cross-sector collaboration, both within municipal departments and across organisations, remain essential. In addition, policy guidelines often lack alternatives for advancing biodiversity in places where infrastructure constraints and urban development limit greening opportunities. Therefore, considering the funding mechanisms the biodiversity's wider ecological, social, health, and climate benefits can help justify difficult spatial decisions, such as reallocating parking space for greenery in Scheveningen or acknowledging the ecological value of parks and forest areas in Rotterdam.

Equally important is improving how collaboration is organised and communicated. The cases showed that residents often struggle to understand municipal procedures, responsibilities, and approval processes. All collaborations should also embed learning through regular reflection, short evaluations, and knowledge-sharing activities across initiatives. Monitoring procedures and biodiversity indicators are also needed at the neighbourhood scale while considering building baseline data so that progress can be assessed and actions adapted when necessary.

Finally, municipalities, residents, and experts could explore ways to better recognise each other's expertise and constraints. This case highlighted the importance of building on existing neighbourhood initiatives to support the adoption of policy ambitions. It also demonstrated the value of connecting designers and planners with resident initiatives, as well as the important role civil servants can play in navigating administrative procedures. Residents interested in supporting such initiatives should be aware that municipal processes often involve delays and require patience, while remaining open to different perspectives on nature and seeking common ground across initiatives.

This task builds on your current understanding of the challenge. Other perspectives may not yet be visible unless they are explored further, for example by using the same questions to engage with or interview other actors.

Choose a challenge: Use the guiding questions of one challenge cluster to explore it in relation with your work or interests.

Shared spaces and collective practices

Who creates and governs these in the future?

Shared spaces are increasingly shaped by tensions between shared resources and privatisation.

Questions to explore

How can new shared spaces be created?

What forms of governance can involve citizens?

Justice and care

Who has access to wellbeing?

Access to health, green space, mobility and safety varies.

Questions to explore

How can territorial inequalities be reduced?

How can overlooked needs become visible?

Vulnerability and climate adaptation:

How can we live with a changing climate?

Places, in for example, cities will face increasing exposure to extreme weather events, resource scarcity and biodiversity loss. Adaptation is not only a technical challenge but also requires new ways of inhabiting and relating to an environment.

Questions to explore

How can one respond to extreme weather and new forms of vulnerability or exposure to harm or risk?

How can disrupted ecological relationships be restored?

How can natural and built systems be better integrated?

How can territories address the challenge without increasing inequalities?

Memory and conflict:

Whose stories shape  transformation?

Regeneration is the process of improving and transforming parts of a place to make them stable locations to live and work. However, it often creates tensions between memories, identities, interests, and different visions of the future, where some stories are highlighted while others are overlooked or erased.

Questions to explore

How can marginalised histories be recognised and valued?

How can conflicts between long-term residents and newcomers be addressed?

How can development avoid pushing aside people’s culture or stories?

How can conflict support transformation?

The right to transform:

Who has the power to shape the future of a place?

Urban transformation is often driven by a limited number of government and economic actors. Yet emerging forms of participation, activism and civic engagement are reshaping who has the power to envision, influence, and shape the future of cities.

Questions to explore

Who is excluded from decisions about the future of a place?

How can participation be broadened and made more meaningful?

Which non-human actors should have a voice in decision-making?

What new forms of democracy could emerge?

Start with your personal connection. Describe a moment where you noticed the challenge. Be specific (e.g. “on my daily commute…” or “in my neighbourhood…”).

Describe why it matters? Explain why this problem is important to you and what consequences does it have for whom.

What does it bother you about this situation? Share what feels wrong, unfair, or unsustainable.

What inspires you to act? Consider also what triggered your interest, positively.

Who is mostly affected by this situation? Mention people, groups, or even the environment affected by this problem situation.

What do you wish it could be different? Share your feelings and observations about the change you wish to see and why is not happening yet.

What photos or visual helps to illustrate the situation? Acknowledge the source and copyrights as necessary.

La Goccia is an 18-hectare former industrial site in Milan, between the Bovisa and Villapizzone neighbourhoods. It is contaminated and has been closed for over 30 years. In that time, nature has turned it into a spontaneous urban forest with more than 15,000 trees and about 40 bird species. The GOCCIA project (Green Opportunities to Clean-up Contaminants through an Interspecies Alliance) aims to complete the clean-up using Nature-Based Solutions. It also aims to test a multispecies model that other cities can reuse.

Creating places where people and other living beings can thrive together.

By Thorsten Philipp & Juliette Cortes-Arevalo

Under preparation

Add caption

Cities and everyday environments are often imagined and designed as spaces made by and for humans. Yet they are continuously inhabited, shaped and transformed by plants, animals, fungi, bacteria and other non-human agents. This module introduces More-than-Human and Multispecies Design as approaches for moving beyond Human-Centred approach and reconsidering Design as a relational practice within interconnected ecological worlds. Learners will explore how anthropocentric assumptions shape urban environments and how non-human agency can be acknowledged in city design. Attention is given to living and non-living agents, whose behaviours, needs and capacities are frequently overlooked despite their central role in urban ecosystems. Through data collection, relationship mapping, reversed perspective approach and future envisioning, learners will identify non-human agents, investigate the relations and stressors that shape its everyday conditions and reflect on existing power dynamics. They will therefore transform the insights gathered into a speculative future scenario “beyond the human”, aimed at fostering a mutually beneficial coexistence between the human and non-human worlds. The module encourages participants to document a contextualised multispecies relationship, to critically question anthropocentric assumptions and to propose an possible intervention that is attentive to coexistence, care, temporality and the autonomy of different forms of life.

Recognise the limits of designing only for humans and why it matters to consider other living beings in the design of shared spaces.

Learn to see a place from the perspective of the plants and animals that live there.

Imagine Imagine a future that supports coexistence between humans and nature.

A day at the first City as a Laboratory Knowledge Exchange Masterclass in a Berlin innovation hub, connecting people across sectors to drive change.

By Tim Noppeney, communications and strategist consultant

The Knowledge Exchange Masterclass

What: A one-day training course in transdisciplinary methods for professionals from business, civil society, public administration, and cultural organisations.

Part of: CAL:TS – The City as a Laboratory, an Erasmus+ co-funded collaboration of TU Berlin, TU Delft, and Politecnico di Milano within the ENHANCE alliance.

2026 edition: Held on 17 September at MotionLab Berlin, with 12 participants. Facilitated by Thorsten Philipp, Nina Schmulius, and Jan Kratzer, with support from City as A Laboratory colleagues Juliette Cortes-Arevalo and Valentina Facoetti.

Methods: User-driven innovation and storytelling were introduced through dedicated activities. Citizen science, real-world and living labs, and service learning were explored through open discussions and a speed-dating format.

Participant feedback: All 10 respondents said the training deepened their understanding of transdisciplinary approaches and that they gained a positive network.

Next edition: Delft, 2 October 2027, with collaborators from the 

VPDelta innovation program.

Keywords

Event category: 

One-day session

Method category: 

Reconstruct & Intervene

Inner Development Goal: 

Relating

Change step:

records.content:
Around the table (Figure 1), many people were heading somewhere new: a business, a PhD, a job. So was I. I’m reorienting myself professionally, and over the years I have collected a lot of diverse educational and professional experiences: ethnology, psychology, business, design, corporate innovation, consulting and, most recently, applied research. I often say that having so many different interests sometimes feel like a liability. It’s hard to focus only on one field when there are so many, and a patchwork CV often doesn’t cover all the requirements in a job ad while leaving many other experiences and skills irrelevant. So, when I read about the CAL:TS project and this masterclass on their website one lazy Friday afternoon, I almost felt understood. The description promised:

"Participants learn how to initiate and run collaborative enquiries with universities, civic actors and users, and how to route results back into organisational decision making."

I mean, for a (wannabe) world-saving Millennial who’s slightly lost in our chaotic times, this sounds ideal. So, I signed up hoping to explore transdisciplinary in a more structured way, to connect with people who share these in-between interests, and to see whether this could be where my private, academic and professional interests finally align.

hierarchy.lvl1: Finding connection in a chaotic world
Finding connection in a chaotic world

records.content: The masterclass took place at MotionLab (Figure 2) and it was kind of the joke of the day that the vibes of the industrial complex where the maker space is located made you want to double-check your kidneys were still there before leaving. Berlin being Berlin. [Flag: keep, soften or cut?] But once you find the beach chairs out front and walk through the towering gate of the maker space, you’re in for a treat: a friendly, slightly quirky reception, then an open warehouse with a coffee area, co-working spaces, 3D printers and an old bus repurposed as a place to meet and relax. Thorsten, one of the organisers, was there to welcome me, and I felt comfortable from the first moment. Like everyone else, I immediately had an itch to try out some of the machinery.

hierarchy.lvl1: Finding connection in a chaotic world
Finding connection in a chaotic world

records.content: Within the first 30 minutes everyone had four genuinely enjoyable conversations (Figure 3), and I arrived late at the first session because of one of them. What hit home first was the feeling of coming home, intellectually speaking. The mixed backgrounds spanned science communication, music, anthropology, business development, startup leadership, design engineering, circular economy and fundraising, and they had all already done so much that I almost felt out of place. Luckily, it was a self-selected and inviting crowd: most of us work in fields driving socio-ecological sustainability, many have moved between disciplines, sectors and roles, and there is a shared desire to organise collaborations and change existing systems in one way or another. Everything seemed to be seeking a way to address complex real-life challenges. And not everyone came for their day job, either. One participant is planning a music festival accompanied by transdisciplinary research. For me, it might become a photography project and hopefully a new career path.

hierarchy.lvl1: Finding connection in a chaotic world
Finding connection in a chaotic world

records.content: I think definitions are foundational to any conversation, so I appreciated starting by going deeper into the histories and facets of trans disciplinarity. Two translations for “trans” struck me as simple and impactful: “through” and “beyond”. Trans disciplinarity shifts the focus and starts from relevant real-world challenges. It brings discipline to that end but doesn’t just add them side by side. Rather, it goes through and beyond disciplines, filling the spaces between them. For many of us, that in-between space, where people and perspectives connect, excites us the most.

hierarchy.lvl1: Finding connection in a chaotic world
Finding connection in a chaotic world

records.content:
After the basics, we explored five methods: citizen science, real-world and living labs, user-driven innovation, storytelling and service learning. They worked as prompts to talk about our own experience, and the conversations went deepest on user-driven innovation (involving users as active innovators), storytelling (as a means to connect, make sense and drive change) and service learning (integrating civic engagement with academic learning).
Personally, I think the storytelling session led by Nina Schmulius was the most fun and useful one. First, we freely wrote for five minutes without a prompt, and judging by the scratchy sounds of pens on paper, nobody was short of things to say. Then we condensed it into an Elfchen, a poem of eleven words. Here is mine where I went from my desire for creativity in the free-writing part to the importance of relationships for that creativity (whatever, okay? don’t judge.):

Relationships That's it Creates us all Whether we know or Not

While service learning posted by Jan Kratzer was also very intriguing, next to the speed-dating conversations we covered almost too many that day. I would have loved to go deeper into one of them and apply it to a real case from my own work or life. Others felt similar, so the organisers are putting this feedback into the next edition.

hierarchy.lvl1: Finding connection in a chaotic world
Finding connection in a chaotic world

records.content:
Reflecting on what the description promised, one day gives you a map, a network and a first taste of initiating collaborative enquiries, not the full toolkit to run them, but I wasn’t expecting that anyway. The masterclass delivered on all those counts because I left with a bunch of contacts and intriguing resources after a thoroughly enjoyable day (including after hours in a maker space. Again, Berlin being Berlin). I think the masterclass is so valuable, I offered the CAL:TS team my help and am now contributing in a volunteering capacity, which anyone else who’s interested can do too. If your many interests sometimes feel more like a liability than a gift and the world seems a bit too complex and overwhelming, go and find your crowd at the next masterclass in Delft. I found mine.
And let’s be honest on that front: relationships and methods from events like this often fade quickly, which is why I’m glad the conversation continues in the Knowledge Exchange community on LinkedIn.
